user_text: A 60,000-person municipal wastewater plant lifts primary sludge with twelve progressive-cavity pumps, each a 10-stage unit whose chrome-plated rotor has a 52-millimetre major diameter and a 26-millimetre minor diameter on a 96-millimetre helical pitch, running inside an NBR stator with 0.6 millimetres of interference fit, at 210 revolutions per minute against a 4.5-bar discharge head, delivering 6.2 cubic metres per hour of 3-percent-solids grit-laden sludge whose dynamic viscosity is about 2,400 millipascal-seconds. The stators wear unevenly at the suction stages where settled grit enters first: volumetric efficiency falls from 92 percent to below 65 percent within nine weeks, the maintenance crew re-stators pumps in rotating confined-space outages costing 4,100 euros per pump, and a stator that seizes past its elastomer limit has twice stalled the hopper mixer long enough to back up the grit channel. We need stator service life held above 26 weeks while keeping volumetric efficiency above 80 percent, on the existing rotor pitch and stage count, without replacing the twelve pump frames or their 5.5-kilowatt drives, without lowering the 6.2-cubic-metre-per-hour lifting duty, and without adding polymer conditioning that would change downstream dewatering chemistry.
